claim: Tryptophan is converted to 5-hydroxytryptophan (5HTP) by tryptophan hydroxylase (Trh in flies and Tph in mammals).
source: 5-HT is synthesized in two steps: the conversion of tryptophan to 5-hydroxytryptophan (5HTP) by tryptophan hydroxylase (Trh in flies and Tph in mammals) (Kuhn et al., 1979), followed by the conversion of 5HTP to 5-HT by aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kuhn et al., 1979, and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: 5HTP is converted to 5-HT by aromatic amino acid decarboxylase.
source: 5-HT is synthesized in two steps: the conversion of tryptophan to 5-hydroxytryptophan (5HTP) by tryptophan hydroxylase (Trh in flies and Tph in mammals) (Kuhn et al., 1979), followed by the conversion of 5HTP to 5-HT by aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kuhn et al., 1979, and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Four receptors were known to be 5-HT receptors in Drosophila when the project started: 5HT1a, 5HT1b, 5HT2 and 5HT7.
source: Four receptors were known to be 5-HT receptors in drosophila when we started this project: 5HT1a, 5HT1b, 5HT2 and 5HT7 (Colas et al., 1995; Saudou et al., 1992; Witz et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Colas et al., 1995; Saudou et al., 1992; Witz et al., 1990.

claim: CG42796 is a new 5-HT receptor named 5HT2b.
source: Our bioinformatics analysis had revealed a new G-protein- coupled receptor (GPCR), annotated as CG42796 in the drosophila genome, as a new 5-HT receptor which we named as 5HT2b, with the previously known 5HT2 becoming 5HT2a (Brody and Cravchik, 2000; Gasque et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatics analysis and citations to Brody and Cravchik, 2000; Gasque et al., 2013.

claim: 5HT2b is predicted to be coupled to Gq protein.
source: 5HT2b was predicted to be coupled to Gq protein and shown in our collaboration to mediate 5-HT responsiveness (Gasque et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a prediction and a citation to Gasque et al., 2013.

claim: 5HT2b mediates 5-HT responsiveness.
source: 5HT2b was predicted to be coupled to Gq protein and shown in our collaboration to mediate 5-HT responsiveness (Gasque et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from a collaboration and a citation to Gasque et al., 2013.

claim: Trh mutant flies slept less than wild type controls.
source: Trh, 5HT1a or 5HT2b mutant flies were found to sleep less than the wt in both 12 hr (hr) light/12 hr dark (LD) cycles and in constant darkness (DD) (Figure 1F–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F–H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: 5HT1a mutant flies slept less than wild type controls.
source: Trh, 5HT1a or 5HT2b mutant flies were found to sleep less than the wt in both 12 hr (hr) light/12 hr dark (LD) cycles and in constant darkness (DD) (Figure 1F–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F–H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: 5HT2b mutant flies slept less than wild type controls.
source: Trh, 5HT1a or 5HT2b mutant flies were found to sleep less than the wt in both 12 hr (hr) light/12 hr dark (LD) cycles and in constant darkness (DD) (Figure 1F–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F–H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: Trh, 5HT1a and 5HT2b mutants exhibited reduced sleep bout duration during the day and night.
source: These three mutants exhibited reduced sleep bout duration during the day and night (Figure 1I), and also in DD phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3D and E.

claim: Trh, 5HT1a and 5HT2b mutants displayed prolonged latency to sleep at night.
source: Trh, 5HT1a and 5HT2b mutants also displayed prolonged latency to sleep at night (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Trh, 5HT1a and 5HT2b mutants showed no change in the intensity of locomotor activity when awake.
source: Trh, 5HT1a and 5HT2b mutants showed no change in the intensity of locomotor activity when awake (Figure 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: 5HT1a mutant flies had reduced sleep.
source: As reported previously, 5HT1a mutant flies had reduced sleep (Yuan et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yuan et al., 2006.

claim: The sleep phenotype of 5HT2b mutants was much more severe than that of 5HT1a mutants, nearly equal to that of Trh mutants.
source: The sleep phenotype of 5HT2b mutants was much more severe than that of 5HT1a mutants, nearly equal to that of Trh mutants (Figure 1E and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and H.

claim: In DD, 5HT2b mutants showed a large decrease in sleep duration and sleep bout duration in both the subjective daytime and the subjective nighttime.
source: In DD, 5HT2b mutants showed a large decrease in sleep duration and sleep bout duration in both the subjective daytime and the subjective nighttime (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: 5HT2b functions to promote sleep.
source: These results indicated that 5HT2b functions to promote sleep.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing reduced sleep in 5HT2b mutants.

claim: Male 5HT1b mutants exhibited decreased sleep during the daytime of LD but not during DD.
source: Results in males were similar to those in females except that male 5HT1b mutants exhibited decreased sleep during the daytime of LD but not during DD (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The difference between LD and DD in 5HT1b mutants was consistent with the abnormal light sensitivity of 5HT1b mutants as reported previously.
source: The difference between LD and DD was consistent with the abnormal light sensitivity of 5HT1b mutants as reported previously (Yuan et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yuan et al., 2005.

claim: Two mg/ml 5HTP for 3 days restored 5HT immunofluorescence in the brains of Trh01 and TrhGKO flies.
source: Two mg/ml 5HTP for 3 days restored 5HT immunofluorescence in the brains of Trh01 and TrhGKO flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–H.

claim: 5-HTP feeding rescued both daytime and nighttime sleep in Trh01 mutants to about wt level.
source: 5-HTP feeding rescued both daytime and nighttime sleep in 5HTP to Trh01 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2I and J) and in TrhGKO mutants (data not shown) to about wt level, indicating that 5-HT promotes sleep in adult flies.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2I and J.

claim: 5-HT promotes sleep in adult flies.
source: 5-HTP feeding rescued both daytime and nighttime sleep in 5HTP to Trh01 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2I and J) and in TrhGKO mutants (data not shown) to about wt level, indicating that 5-HT promotes sleep in adult flies.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that 5-HTP feeding restores sleep in Trh mutants.

claim: The involvement of 5-HT in circadian rhythm has been reported previously.
source: The involvement of 5-HT in circadian rhythm has been reported previously (Nichols, 2007; Page, 1987; Rea et al., 1994; Yuan et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nichols, 2007; Page, 1987; Rea et al., 1994; Yuan et al., 2005.

claim: No circadian period changes were observed in any of the mutants when compared to the wt in the same genetic background.
source: We have not observed circadian period changes in any of our mutants when compared to the wt in the same genetic background after entrainment to a 12 hr (hr) light/12 hr dark (LD) cycle for 3 days, followed by analysis in constant darkness (DD) for 12 days (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Trh and 5HT2b mutants exhibited a significantly lower percentage of sleep recovery rate than wt flies.
source: Trh and 5HT2b mutants exhibited a significantly lower percentage of sleep recovery rate than wt flies (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: 5HT1a mutant flies, though defective in sleep, were similar to the wt and mutants of any other serotonergic receptors in showing normal sleep recovery after sleep deprivation.
source: However, 5HT1a mutant flies, though defective in sleep, were similar to the wt and mutants of any other serotonergic receptors in showing normal sleep recovery after sleep deprivation (Figure 2A and B), further supporting the hypothesis that involvement in regulating total sleep time is separate from involvement in regulating sleep recovery after deprivation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Involvement in regulating total sleep time is separate from involvement in regulating sleep recovery after deprivation.
source: However, 5HT1a mutant flies, though defective in sleep, were similar to the wt and mutants of any other serotonergic receptors in showing normal sleep recovery after sleep deprivation (Figure 2A and B), further supporting the hypothesis that involvement in regulating total sleep time is separate from involvement in regulating sleep recovery after deprivation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that 5HT1a mutants have reduced sleep but normal sleep recovery.

claim: 5HTP restored sleep homeostasis in Trh mutant flies to the normal level.
source: We found that 5HTP restored sleep homeostasis in Trh mutant flies to the normal level (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: 5-HT functions to control sleep homeostasis in adult flies and not through indirect actions during development.
source: To test whether 5-HT functions to control sleep homeostasis in adult flies and not through indirect actions during development, we fed 5-HTP to adult flies. We found that 5HTP restored sleep homeostasis in Trh mutant flies to the normal level (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that 5-HTP feeding in adult flies restores sleep homeostasis in Trh mutants.

claim: Trh and 5HT2b mutant flies showed impaired sleep recovery when compared to wt flies after sleep loss induced by activation of dopaminergic neurons.
source: We measured the sleep loss, sleep gain and recovery rate in wt, Trh mutant and 5HT2b mutant flies after sleep loss induced by activation of dopaminergic neurons. Trh and 5HT2b mutant flies showed impaired sleep recovery when compared to wt flies (Figure 2E–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E–J.

claim: 5-HT and its 2b receptor regulate sleep homeostasis in adult flies, independent of the methods of sleep deprivation.
source: Thus, our results indicate that 5-HT and its 2b receptor regulate sleep homeostasis in adult flies, independent of the methods of sleep deprivation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Trh and 5HT2b mutants show impaired sleep recovery after both mechanical and thermogenetic sleep deprivation.

claim: Trh::Gal4 labeled all of the previously reported 5-HT clusters in the adult brain.
source: Trh::Gal4 labeled all of the previously reported 5-HT clusters in the adult brain: Anterior lateral protocerebrum (ALP), Anterior medial protocerebrum (AMP), Anterior dorsomedial protocerebrum (ADMP), Lateral protocerebrum (LP), Lateral subesophageal ganglion (SEL) and Medial subesophageal ganglion (SEM) anterior clusters; Posterior lateral protocerebrum (PLP), Posterior medial protocerebrum, dorsal (PMPD), Posterior medial protocerebrum, medial (PMPM) and Posterior medial protocerebrum, ventral (PMPV) posterior clusters (Alekseyenko et al., 2010; Pooryasin and Fiala, 2015; Sitaraman et al., 2008 , 2012; Vallés and White, 1988) and showed similar expression pattern when compared to reported transgenic strains (Alekseyenko et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Alekseyenko et al., 2010; Pooryasin and Fiala, 2015; Sitaraman et al., 2008, 2012; Vallés and White, 1988.

claim: The distribution of the axons and dendrites of neurons that were positive for Trh::Gal4 could be found in the optic lobe, the olfactory lobe, the central complex and the mushroom bodies (MBs).
source: The distribution of the axons and dendrites of neurons that were positive for Trh::Gal4 could be found in the optic lobe, the olfactory lobe, the central complex and the mushroom bodies (MBs) (Figure 3C and D, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D, and Video 1.

claim: 5HT2b::Gal4 labeled more than 500 neurons in the brain.
source: 5HT2b::Gal4 labeled more than 500 neurons in the brain (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The axons and dendrites of 5HT2b-positive neurons were found in the central complex, the olfactory lobe, the optic lobe, the subesophageal ganglion and the ventrolateral protocerebrum, but not the MBs.
source: The axons and dendrites were found in the central complex, the olfactory lobe, the optic lobe, the subesophageal ganglion and the ventrolateral protocerebrum, but not the MBs (Figure 3G and H, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and H, and Video 2.

claim: A recent study of 5HT2b expression using the MiMIC system labeled the same brain regions and showed a similar expression pattern.
source: A recent study of 5HT2b expression using the MiMIC system labeled the same brain regions and showed a similar expression pattern (Gnerer et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gnerer et al., 2015.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of either 5HT2b or dFB neurons reduced sleep relative to controls.
source: RNAi-mediated knockdown of either 5HT2b or dFB neurons reduced sleep relative to controls, whereas knockdown of 5HT2b in other regions had no significant effect (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Knockdown of 5HT2b in other regions had no significant effect on sleep.
source: RNAi-mediated knockdown of either 5HT2b or dFB neurons reduced sleep relative to controls, whereas knockdown of 5HT2b in other regions had no significant effect (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 23E10-GAL4 and 23E10-LexA lines labeled approximately 40 neurons projecting their axons to the dFB.
source: 23E10-GAL4 and 23E10-LexA lines labeled approximately 40 neurons projecting their axons to the dFB (Figure 4B and C) (Donlea et al., 2014; Manning et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C, and citations to Donlea et al., 2014; Manning et al., 2012.

claim: Two to four dFB neurons were labeled on each side of the adult fly with intersection of 5HT2b and 23E10.
source: Two to four dFB neurons were labeled on each side of the adult fly with intersection of 5HT2b and 23E10 (Figure 4D and E, Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and E, and Video 3.

claim: Only a single dFB neuron on each side of the adult fly was positive for both green fluorescent protein (GFP) and red fluorescent protein (RFP).
source: We also used 23E10-Gal4 and 5HT2b-LexA to drive the expression of UAS-StingerGFP and LexAop-tdTomato separately (Figure 4F). Only a single dFB neuron on each side of the adult fly was positive for both green fluorescent protein (GFP) and red fluorescent protein (RFP) (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F, G, and H.

claim: A single pair of 5HT2b-positive neurons exist in the dFB.
source: They constitute a single pair of 5HT2b-positive neurons in the dFB.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that only one neuron on each side is positive for both 5HT2b and 23E10 markers.

claim: The pattern of 5HT2b protein expression was similar to that of 5HT2b gene expression.
source: To visualize 5HT2b protein expression, we constructed a 5HT2b protein-trap knockin strain by fusing a superfolder GFP to the carboxyl terminus of 5HT2b protein (Pédelacq et al., 2006). We found the pattern of protein expression to be similar to that of 5HT2b gene expression (Figure 3E and Figure 4J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 4J, and a citation to Pédelacq et al., 2006.

claim: Both strong anti-serotonin immunofluorescence and 5HT2bsfGFP staining signal were found in the dorsal FB region.
source: We also found both strong anti-serotonin immunofluorescence and 5HT2bsfGFP staining signal in the dorsal FB region (Figure 4I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I–K.

claim: Strong GFP was found in the presynaptic region of ExFl2 neurons, but not in the postsynaptic region nor in the cell body.
source: To determine whether the ExFl2 neurons contribute to the 5HT2bsfGFP staining signal in the dorsal FB region, we crossed UAS-5HT2bsfGFP to 23E10-Gal4, and found strong GFP in the presynaptic region of ExFl2 neurons, but not in the postsynaptic region nor in the cell body (Figure 4L–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4L–N.

claim: The 5HT2b receptor is located presynaptically in ExFl2 neurons.
source: These results suggest that the 5HT2b receptor is located presynaptically in ExFl2 neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that 5HT2bsfGFP is found in the presynaptic region but not in the postsynaptic region or cell body of ExFl2 neurons.

claim: Artificial activation of dFB neurons induces sleep.
source: Artificial activation of dFB neurons induces sleep (Donlea et al., 2011; Ueno et al., 2012), whereas silencing of them reduces sleep (Kottler et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Donlea et al., 2011; Ueno et al., 2012.

claim: Silencing of dFB neurons reduces sleep.
source: Artificial activation of dFB neurons induces sleep (Donlea et al., 2011; Ueno et al., 2012), whereas silencing of them reduces sleep (Kottler et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kottler et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2012.

claim: Sleep duration was reduced in flies in which 23E10 neurons were ablated.
source: Sleep duration was reduced in flies in which 23E10 neurons were ablated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Flies without 23E10 neurons lost sleep homeostasis: showing no sleep rebound after 12-hr overnight sleep deprivation.
source: Flies without 23E10 neurons lost sleep homeostasis: showing no sleep rebound after 12-hr overnight sleep deprivation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: Sleep was greatly increased after 23E10 and 5HT2b intersectional neurons were activated.
source: Sleep was greatly increased after 23E10 and 5HT2b intersectional neurons were activated (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: Sleep was reduced in flies in which 23E10 and 5HT2b intersectional neurons were ablated.
source: Sleep was reduced in flies in which 23E10 and 5HT2b intersectional neurons were ablated (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: Sleep homeostasis was impaired after ablation of 23E10 and 5HT2b intersectional neurons.
source: Sleep homeostasis was impaired after ablation of 23E10 and 5HT2b intersectional neurons (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D–F.

claim: 5HT2b expression in all 5HT2b positive neurons significantly increased sleep duration at nighttime but did not affect daytime sleep.
source: 5HT2bGKO is a Gal4 KI line generated by Strategy II which was used to drive the expression of 5HT2b cDNA in all 5HT2b neurons, whereas 23E10 Gal4 was used to drive 5HT2b expression in dFB neurons (Figure 6A). Both significantly increased sleep duration at nighttime but neither affected daytime sleep (Figure 6B and C), indicating that 5HT2b in dFB neurons is sufficient to promote nighttime sleep.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, B, and C.

claim: 5HT2b expression in dFB neurons significantly increased sleep duration at nighttime but did not affect daytime sleep.
source: 5HT2bGKO is a Gal4 KI line generated by Strategy II which was used to drive the expression of 5HT2b cDNA in all 5HT2b neurons, whereas 23E10 Gal4 was used to drive 5HT2b expression in dFB neurons (Figure 6A). Both significantly increased sleep duration at nighttime but neither affected daytime sleep (Figure 6B and C), indicating that 5HT2b in dFB neurons is sufficient to promote nighttime sleep.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, B, and C.

claim: 5HT2b in dFB neurons is sufficient to promote nighttime sleep.
source: Both significantly increased sleep duration at nighttime but neither affected daytime sleep (Figure 6B and C), indicating that 5HT2b in dFB neurons is sufficient to promote nighttime sleep.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that 5HT2b expression in dFB neurons increases nighttime sleep.

claim: Sleep recovery after 12-hr deprivation in 5HT2b mutant flies was rescued by either 5HT2b expression in all 5HT2b positive neurons or 5HT2b expression in 23E10 neurons.
source: Sleep recovery after 12-hr deprivation in 5HT2b mutant flies was rescued by either 5HT2b expression in all 5HT2b positive neurons or 5HT2b expression in 23E10 neurons (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: A dFB gene knockdown strain showed shortened sleep duration and impaired sleep homeostasis.
source: We also used RNAi knockdown of the 5HT2b gene in dFB neurons to test the necessity of 5HT2b. A dFB gene knockdown strain showed shortened sleep duration and impaired sleep homeostasis (Figure 6K–O).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6K–O.

claim: 5HT2b in dFB neurons is sufficient to regulate sleep homeostasis.
source: These results indicate that 5HT2b in dFB neurons is sufficient to regulate sleep homeostasis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that 5HT2b expression in dFB neurons restores sleep homeostasis in 5HT2b mutants.

claim: The sleep duration of flies in which 5HT2bGKO drove the expression of 5HT2b cDNA in all 5HT2b neurons except one pair of dFB neurons, in the 5HT2b knockout background was significantly decreased, to a level similar to that of the 5HT2b knockout mutants.
source: The sleep duration of flies in which 5HT2bGKO drove the expression of 5HT2b cDNA in all 5HT2b neurons. except one pair of dFB neurons, in the 5HT2b knockout background was significantly decreased, to a level similar to that of the 5HT2b knockout mutants (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: Flies lacking 5HT2b receptor in dFB neurons had no sleep recovery after 12-hr deprivation.
source: Furthermore, flies lacking 5HT2b receptor in dFB neurons had no sleep recovery after 12-hr deprivation (Figure 6I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I and J.

claim: Both sleep duration and homeostasis were restored in the strain with 5HT2b rescued with Gal80 in dFB neurons in the background of 5HT2b knockdown.
source: In addition, we rescued the expression of 5HT2b with Gal80 in dFB neurons in the background of 5HT2b knockdown to test the sufficiency of 5HT2b. Both sleep duration and homeostasis were restored in this strain (Figure 6K–O).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6K–O.

claim: 5HT2b in a small subset, probably a single pair, of dFB neurons is necessary for the regulation of sleep homeostasis.
source: These results indicate that 5HT2b in a small subset, probably a single pair, of dFB neurons is necessary for the regulation of sleep homeostasis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experiments showing that removing 5HT2b from one pair of dFB neurons abolishes sleep homeostasis.

claim: The 5HT2b receptor is required in one pair of dFB neurons to regulate sleep homeostasis.
source: Our results indicate that the 5HT2b receptor is required in one pair of dFB neurons to regulate sleep homeostasis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that 5HT2b in one pair of dFB neurons is necessary and sufficient for sleep homeostasis.

claim: The total amount of sleep and sleep recovery after deprivation may involve different mechanisms.
source: Our finding of the differential roles of the receptors in promoting sleep and in regulating sleep recovery clearly show that the total amount of sleep and sleep recovery after deprivation may involve different mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that 5HT1a mutants have reduced sleep but normal sleep recovery, while 5HT2b mutants have both reduced sleep and impaired sleep recovery.

claim: dFB neurons have been shown to be important in sleep.
source: dFB neurons have been shown to be important in sleep (Donlea et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Donlea et al., 2014.

claim: Serotonergic signaling is crucial for sleep regulation.
source: Our results not only reveal that serotonergic signaling is crucial but also show that the expression of 5HT2b in a very small subset of dFB neurons is necessary and sufficient and explain the function of the 5HT2b receptor in sleep regulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that 5HT2b in dFB neurons is necessary and sufficient for sleep homeostasis.

claim: The expression of 5HT2b in a very small subset of dFB neurons is necessary and sufficient for sleep regulation.
source: Our results not only reveal that serotonergic signaling is crucial but also show that the expression of 5HT2b in a very small subset of dFB neurons is necessary and sufficient and explain the function of the 5HT2b receptor in sleep regulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that 5HT2b in one pair of dFB neurons is necessary and sufficient for sleep homeostasis.

claim: The intersectional strategy may involve protein expression at an immature developmental stage, whereas the drivers in the non-intersectional strategy directly showed expression in mature neurons.
source: This could be due to the possibility that the intersectional strategy may involve protein expression at an immature developmental stage, whereas the drivers in the non-intersectional strategy directly showed expression in mature neurons.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning to explain the difference between intersectional and non-intersectional labeling results.

claim: Sleep is also regulated by dopamine and its G-protein-coupled receptor DopR in PPL1 and PPM3 clusters.
source: Sleep is also regulated by dopamine and its G-protein-coupled receptor DopR in PPL1 and PPM3 clusters (Liu et al., 2012; Ueno et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2012; Ueno et al., 2012.

claim: Two separate excitatory synaptic microcircuits oppositely regulate sleep.
source: Two separate excitatory synaptic microcircuits oppositely regulate sleep, and the activity of the sleep-promoting microcircuit in the MB is increased after sleep deprivation (Aso et al., 2014; Sitaraman et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aso et al., 2014; Sitaraman et al., 2015.

claim: The activity of the sleep-promoting microcircuit in the MB is increased after sleep deprivation.
source: Two separate excitatory synaptic microcircuits oppositely regulate sleep, and the activity of the sleep-promoting microcircuit in the MB is increased after sleep deprivation (Aso et al., 2014; Sitaraman et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aso et al., 2014; Sitaraman et al., 2015.

claim: A subset of EB neurons encode sleep drive by modulating calcium level and synaptic strength.
source: A subset of EB neurons encode sleep drive by modulating calcium level and synaptic strength (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: Mutants exhibited normal circadian periods.
source: Mutants exhibited normal circadian periods, but we could not rule out other circadian rhythm defects, such as circadian entrainment.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no circadian period changes in mutants.

claim: It has been reported that 5HT1a mutants have slight reduced recovery sleep after 6 hr of sleep deprivation.
source: It has been reported that 5HT1a mutants have slight reduced recovery sleep after 6 hr of sleep deprivation (Yuan et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yuan et al., 2006.

claim: Normal sleep rebound was found after 12-hr sleep deprivation in 5HT1a mutants.
source: In this study, however, we found normal sleep rebound after 12-hr sleep deprivation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from this study.

claim: Wild type 5-HT level was probably saturated for sleep recovery.
source: In the sleep-recovery experiment, we observed no significant difference between wt flies fed with mock or 5HTP, which indicated that wt 5-HT level was probably saturated for sleep recovery.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that 5HTP feeding does not increase sleep recovery in wild type flies.

claim: Sleep rebound could be dissociated from the baseline sleep.
source: Although the daytime sleep of mutant flies with 5HTP rescue was higher than that of the wt, there was still room for increase if the recovery ability of the flies is restored. Therefore sleep rebound could be dissociated from the baseline sleep.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that 5HTP rescue increases baseline sleep but also restores sleep rebound in mutants.

claim: The role of 5-HT in sleep is controversial in mammals.
source: In mammals, the role of 5-HT in sleep is controversial.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the literature on 5-HT and sleep in mammals.

claim: Early results from lesion and neuropharmacological studies had implicated 5-HT in the initiation and maintenance of slow wave sleep (SWS).
source: Early results from lesion and neuropharmacological studies had implicated 5-HT in the initiation and maintenance of slow wave sleep (SWS) (Jouvet, 1972) , but other reports challenged the serotonergic hypothesis of sleep promotion (Monti, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jouvet, 1972.

claim: Other reports challenged the serotonergic hypothesis of sleep promotion.
source: Early results from lesion and neuropharmacological studies had implicated 5-HT in the initiation and maintenance of slow wave sleep (SWS) (Jouvet, 1972) , but other reports challenged the serotonergic hypothesis of sleep promotion (Monti, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Monti, 2011.

claim: Recent papers claimed that the observed changes in sleep were indirect as resulted from 5-HT involvement in thermoregulation when all serotonergic neurons were genetically deleted in mice.
source: Recent papers claimed that the observed changes in sleep were indirect as resulted from 5-HT involvement in thermoregulation when all serotonergic neurons were genetically deleted in mice (Buchanan and Richerson, 2010; Hodges et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Buchanan and Richerson, 2010; Hodges et al., 2008.

claim: Sleep was decreased in Tph2–/– mice, in which serotonin could not be synthesized in the brain but with normal thermoregulation.
source: Our unpublished data revealed that sleep was decreased in Tph2–/– mice, in which serotonin could not be synthesized in the brain but with normal thermoregulation (Yan HM and YR).
evidence: The claim is supported by unpublished data from the authors.
